paras: The Shawneetown horse thieves shootout was a gunfight near Shawneetown, Indian Territory, reported on April 10, 1888, in which a deputy United States marshal and Sac and Fox Indian police pursued three Black men accused of stealing horses from a Shawnee man named Long Tom. Two of the accused men and one Indian policeman were reported killed and the marshal badly wounded, though one condensed copy of the dispatch put the police dead at two. The story ran widely as a telegraph item, and a longer version joined it to a lynching of horse thieves on the Kansas border that another dispatch reported separately.

Every account came from a single dispatch dated at Oklahoma, Indian Territory, on April 10, relaying the report of a courier from Shawneetown, a settlement on the North Fork of the Canadian River. Most copies placed Shawneetown thirty or forty miles east of Oklahoma, while the longer version located it "in No-Man's-Land."

According to the courier, three "colored horse thieves" took a bunch of horses belonging to Long Tom, described as a Shawnee Indian. When the theft was discovered, a deputy United States marshal rode after them with Sac and Fox Indian police, three in number in most copies. In the officers' account, the only one printed, the men opened fire with Winchester rifles when overtaken and unhorsed one policeman with the first shots. In the "regular pitched battle" that followed, two of the Black men were killed, and an Indian policeman was killed outright or, in the longer version, mortally wounded and died soon after. The marshal was badly wounded, and the horses were recovered.

None of the copies said what became of the third man, and none named the dead men or the policeman. The fight itself was not dated: the short version called it a killing that had "just occurred," while one copy dated the theft "last week" and another "a few weeks ago."
No report of an inquest, arrests or official inquiry into the deaths appears in the coverage.

The story spread by telegraph in a short form and a long "Oklahoma special." The short version ran on April 11 and 12 in papers from St. Paul to Fort Worth, Emporia and Austin, and the following week in the Louisville Weekly Courier-Journal and the Butler Weekly Times. Its headlines cast the episode as outlaws against lawmen and named the race of the dead, as in the Fort Worth Gazette's "Two Negro Horse Thieves and an Indian Police Killed" and the Austin paper's "Negroes and Indians."

The longer version, headlined in the New-York Tribune "Lawlessness in No-Man's-Land" and "A Fight Between Police and Horse Thieves Followed by Wholesale Lynching," reached the Washington Evening Star on April 12 and weeklies in Michigan and Dakota by April 18 and 19. It called the hangings "summary justice" carried out by "avengers" and predicted that the men in the dugout "will undoubtedly be hanged," with no criticism of the ranchmen. The papers printed the officers' version of the fight as fact, and no account from the men pursued or from any other witness appeared.

Most copies reported one Indian policeman killed, but the condensed version carried by the Omaha Daily Bee and later the Iowa County Democrat said two Indian police died. The Oklahoma special added that after the fight fifty ranchmen from the Kansas border caught four horse thieves and hanged them, then besieged six more in a dugout. The Evening Star called the four hanged men "negroes," which would raise the Black dead to six, but the other copies of the special gave no race for them.

A Woodward item relayed from Kansas City, printed in the Omaha Daily Bee on the same page as the fight, described those hangings with no reference to Shawneetown. It credited them to forty farmers from Ashland and other Kansas towns who went into "No Man's Land" "last week," hanged four horse thieves and had nine more barricaded in the Cherokee strip. Because that dispatch dated the hangings to the week before the Shawneetown report and tied them to Kansas farmers, the Oklahoma special appears to have joined two separate episodes.

framing.detail: Short copies ran the officers' account as fact under headlines naming race ('Negroes and Indians'; 'Two Negro Horse Thieves and an Indian Police Killed') and closed with 'The country is overrun with desperadoes and horse thieves.'
The long version called the hangings 'summary justice' by 'avengers' and predicted the besieged men 'will undoubtedly be hanged,' with no criticism.
